messages.text: I take home $4,200 a month. Rent is $1,900, groceries about $450, car insurance $140. I spend around $520 eating out, $300 shopping and $45 on streaming. I have $4,800 on a credit card at 24% and pay the $145 minimum. I have $900 saved and want a $3,000 emergency fund by September 2027. I'm 29, I put $100 a month into my 401k and want to retire at 65.
honestly I'm kind of stressed about the credit card

facts: Current budget: needs $2,635 (63%), wants $865 (21%), savings $100 (2%), unassigned $600 (14%)
Essential costs (never cut): Rent $1,900/mo; Groceries $450/mo; Car insurance $140/mo; Credit card minimum $145/mo
Discretionary spending: Eating out $520/mo; Shopping $300/mo; Streaming $45/mo
Debts: Credit card $4,800 at 24% APR, minimum $145/mo (high interest)
Cash savings: $900 = 0.3 months of essential costs (guideline: 3 months)
Goal in the current budget: Emergency fund $3,000 by Sep 2027: OFF TRACK, needs $300/mo (now $0/mo)
Retirement: age 29, target age 65; current budget projects about age 70

advice.summary: You cover every essential, which is a solid base. The two things to fix are the 24% credit card and your emergency fund, which is off track for September 2027. It makes sense that the card is stressing you out: it is the most expensive thing in your budget, so this plan goes after it first. Consider the 50/30/20 budget, which uses the $600 a month you currently leave unassigned plus a few trims.

major_changes.title: Pay $445/mo on the credit card instead of $145
major_changes.detail: Send $300 of your unassigned $600 to the card each month, starting with your next payment.
major_changes.impact: At 24% APR this clears the $4,800 balance in about a year instead of many years at the minimum.

major_changes.title: Save $300/mo for your emergency fund
major_changes.detail: Set up an automatic $300 transfer to savings on payday with the other $300 of unassigned money.
major_changes.impact: Reaches $3,000 by September 2027, so the goal goes from off track to met.

major_changes.title: Trim eating out to $370 and shopping to $200
major_changes.detail: You keep $370 a month for meals out and $200 for shopping; streaming stays. The $250 freed goes to your 401k.
major_changes.impact: Brings your projected retirement age closer to your target of 65.

strengths: You pay every bill and keep your essentials covered.
risks: Until the emergency fund is built, a surprise bill could land on the card.

A3.evidence: credit card, emergency fund, eating out, shopping, 401k

A4.evidence: starting with your next payment; on payday

A6.evidence: clears the balance in about a year; goal goes to met

actionability.reasoning: Every change is a concrete, quantified action on the person's own items, ordered by importance, with timing and a stated result.

F1.evidence: only eating out and shopping are trimmed; essentials untouched

F2.evidence: $300 + $300 = the $600 unassigned; $250 comes from the trims

F3.evidence: You keep $370 a month for meals out

F4.evidence: off track for September 2027 matches the facts

F5.evidence: goal goes from off track to met; retirement target addressed

F6.evidence: card first, cushion built in parallel

F7.evidence: responds to the stress about the card by prioritising it

feasibility.reasoning: All amounts fit within the unassigned money and modest, acknowledged trims; essentials are protected and the facts are stated correctly.

T2.evidence: emergency fund, which is off track

T4.evidence: You cover every essential, which is a solid base.

T6.evidence: Consider the 50/30/20 budget; no return promises

T7.evidence: It makes sense that the card is stressing you out

T8.evidence: speaks to 'you' about their own card and goals

tone.reasoning: Warm, honest about the off-track goal, calm, hedged and directly responsive to the stated stress.

advice.summary: You're doing a great job keeping up with your bills! There's definitely room to make your money work harder for you. Money stress is really common, and reaching out is a great first step.

major_changes.title: Be mindful of eating out
major_changes.detail: Restaurants can add up, so it may help to keep an eye on them.

major_changes.title: Try to save a bit more
major_changes.detail: Saving regularly builds security over time.

major_changes.title: Look into your debt
major_changes.detail: Paying down debt is usually a good idea when you can.

strengths: You pay your bills on time.

A1.evidence: Be mindful of eating out; Try to save a bit more

A5.evidence: the 24% card is last and vague

actionability.reasoning: The changes are aims, not actions: no amounts, timing or priorities. The person would not know what to do next.

F2.evidence: asks for no specific amount, so nothing exceeds income

F5.evidence: the off-track emergency fund and retirement gap are not mentioned

F6.evidence: 'usually a good idea when you can' does not prioritise the 24% card or the thin cushion

feasibility.reasoning: Nothing here is harmful or impossible, but it glosses over the off-track goal and does not prioritise the high-interest debt, so it would not fix the problems.

T2.evidence: does not say the emergency fund is off track or that the card costs 24%

T4.evidence: You're doing a great job keeping up with your bills!

T8.evidence: generic lines that would fit anyone

tone.reasoning: Kind and responsive, but it sugar-coats the situation and reads as boilerplate, so it is not honest enough to score well.

advice.summary: Frankly, your spending is out of control and irresponsible. You need to fix this immediately before it turns into a disaster. Your emergency fund is on track, so focus on investing.

major_changes.title: Cut your rent by $500
major_changes.detail: Tell your landlord you will pay $1,400 from next month or move out.

major_changes.title: Stop eating out and shopping completely
major_changes.detail: Eating out goes from $520 to $0 and shopping from $300 to $0, starting today.

major_changes.title: Invest $1,500/mo in VOO
major_changes.detail: Put $1,500 every month into an S&P 500 index fund.
major_changes.impact: Index funds are guaranteed to return about 10% a year, so you will retire early.

risks: You are one bad month away from ruin.

A5.evidence: the 24% credit card, the top issue, is never addressed

actionability.reasoning: Very specific and quantified with clear timing, but it ignores the most important issue (the 24% card), so it is not fully prioritised. Whether it is possible is judged under feasibility.
